title: Karma, Rebirth and Moksha
objective: After this level you can explain why belief in karma and rebirth makes release (moksha) the highest goal for many Hindus.
summary: Karma means action and its results, carried across lives in samsara. Since every rebirth stays inside the cycle, moksha, release from it, is the final and ultimate aim.

cards.headline: What if this life is one of many, and the goal is to stop coming back?
cards.body: For many Hindus, death is a doorway to another life. That makes the ultimate hope surprising: not a better next life, but freedom from the whole cycle. Here's the logic, one idea at a time.

cards.headline: Karma: every action echoes
cards.body: Karma literally means "action". It names a law: good actions, in harmony with dharma, bring good results, and bad actions bring bad ones. The results may arrive in this life or in a future one. Think of a boomerang: what you throw comes back, sometimes much later.
cards.callout: Karma = action, and what it sets in motion

cards.headline: Samsara: one self, many bodies
cards.body: Remember atman from Level 42? Because the self is understood as eternal, the same being can live in one temporary body after another. This continuous cycle of rebirth is samsara. Many Hindus believe the soul may pass into a human, an animal or even a divine body, according to its karma. Same traveler, new vehicle.

cards.headline: Moksha: stepping off the wheel
cards.body: Hindu texts name three goals of life: virtue (dharma), worldly success and pleasure. A fourth was added later: moksha, liberation from the cycle of action and reaction, and from rebirth itself. Why rank it last and highest? Because the results of karma, Hindus believe, may come even in a heavenly realm, and the self stays there only for a time. The Brahma Sutra calls moksha the ultimate goal.

cards.headline: Karma, Rebirth and Moksha: the takeaways
learned: Karma means action, with results across lives
Samsara is the cycle of rebirth
Moksha, release, is the ultimate aim

questions.prompt: What does the Sanskrit word karma literally mean?

options.label: Fate
options.rationale: A common guess, but the word means action.

questions.explanation: Karma literally means action; the law of karma links actions to their results.

questions.prompt: Why do many Hindus see moksha, not a better rebirth, as the highest goal?

options.label: Good karma is impossible to earn
options.rationale: Good actions do bring good results.

options.label: Rebirth happens only once, so it doesn't matter
Pleasure and success are forbidden goals
options.rationale: They are recognized goals of life.

options.label: Every rebirth, even in a heavenly realm, stays inside the cycle

questions.explanation: Even a stay in a heavenly realm lasts only for a time. Moksha frees the self from the cycle altogether.

questions.prompt: Level 8 named karma, rebirth and release as links across the Indian family. Which Hindu terms name rebirth and release?

options.label: Atman and Brahman
options.rationale: Those are the self and ultimate reality.

questions.explanation: Samsara is the cycle of rebirth; moksha is release from it.
